What the data says

Readers who get past the first 10% mostly finish. This book loses more readers in Chapter 12 than anywhere else after the opening.

Of 171,400 readers who opened the book, 68.0% carried past the first 10%. Of those, 67.6% reached the last page. The one exception to an otherwise flat middle is a single step down in Chapter 12.

Comparable titles means 1,240 titles: psychological thriller, 300–400 standardized KU pages, enrolled in Kindle Unlimited, within their first 18 months after publication. The cohort is never a single named title.

Read-through curve

Share of readers who opened the book and are still reading at each position. The chart shows where readers stop. It does not know what happens there.

Keyboard: focus the chart, then ← → to move 1%, Shift + arrow for 5%, Home and End for the ends.

About the first 10% band. 10% is the Kindle Unlimited threshold used here for the opening stretch. It is related to the free sample but not the same thing. Sample length varies by title, so a reader stopping in this band has not necessarily stopped at the end of a sample.

    An upper bound, not a forecast. It assumes readers retained through Chapter 12 go on to read like readers who already got past it. Some would have stopped later anyway. Treat it as the size of the opportunity, not the size of the gain. Whether to show authors a figure like this at all is still open, as is which counterfactual it should rest on. That is a product call, not an analytics one, so this panel sits outside the pilot until Product decides.

    Compare your titles

    Both titles measured over their first 90 days after publication. Comparing a two-year-old title against a three-month-old one would not mean anything, so the window is aligned.

    The Teacher has the worse opening. It loses 4 more points inside the first 10%. After that it has no mid-book step down of the kind this book has in Chapter 12, and it ends 1 point higher at 47%. Two different problems: one is an opening problem, the other is a Chapter 12 problem.

    Read this panel with the most caution. It depends on series metadata. Independently published series often have series fields unset or ordered inconsistently, so book order cannot always be trusted. This is the part of the concept that needs the most work before it could ship.

    What you see, and what you never see

    Reading Insights reports patterns across many readers. It does not report people.

    ✔ You can see

    Aggregated across many readers, with small groups suppressed.

    • ✔ The aggregated read-through curve for your title
    • ✔ Where drop-off concentrates, by chapter or by page
    • ✔ The share who borrowed the book and never opened it
    • ✔ Month-to-month movement on these numbers
    • ✔ Read-through into the next book of your own series
    • ✔ Benchmarks against a cohort of comparable titles, never a named title

    🔒 You never see

    Reader-level data does not leave the aggregate.

    • ✕ Any individual reader, or anything traceable to one
    • ✕ A named reader’s progress, highlights, notes or bookmarks
    • ✕ Reader age, gender, or location finer than marketplace
    • ✕ Anything a reader read outside your own titles
    • ✕ A named competitor’s curve
    • ✕ Any figure resting on fewer than N readers. N is a policy placeholder and has not been agreed.

    Methodology and caveats

    The limits are on the page, not in a footnote.

    1. Pilot covers top titles only. Low-volume titles are suppressed.
    2. Kindle Unlimited borrowers, not buyers. Reading on purchased copies is technically reachable but is out of scope for the pilot.
    3. Positions are standardized KU pages (KENPC) measured from the Start Reading Location. They are not manuscript pages and not print pages.
    4. Revising and re-uploading recalculates KENPC, which moves the ruler. Curves on either side of a revision are not directly comparable.
    5. In-progress reads look like drop-offs. Only borrows older than 30 days are counted.
    6. First-time pages only. Re-reads are excluded, and there is a 3,000-page cap per reader per title.
    7. Whispersync syncs the furthest location on reconnect, so read depth can be overstated.
    8. The most recent period is incomplete. Reading and royalty data settles about 45 days after month end.
    9. The comparable-titles cohort has a minimum size, and its definition is shown on screen so the comparison can be judged.
    10. Series read-through depends on series metadata. Ordering is unreliable where series fields are unset.
    11. Every figure on this page is illustrative.
